task: Write one sentence of your own using the word dither. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know dither should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Standing at the trailhead map, the hikers dithered between the ridge loop and the falls path until the morning fog burned off.
To hesitate is milder than to dither — a single beat of doubt before you move.
Freeze goes further than dither: the fussing stops and nothing moves at all.

To waver is to falter briefly in your resolve — a moment's wobble before you steady yourself and go on. Dither is longer and fussier: wavering passes, while dithering is drawn-out indecision that keeps circling the choice without ever landing on it.

To stall is to delay on purpose, buying time — the person stalling has already decided what they want and is playing for position. Dither is the opposite failure: a ditherer delays because they genuinely cannot decide, fussing at the choice with no tactic behind it.
to land on a choice
to bind yourself to a course and stay

Dither comes from Middle English didderen, 'to tremble or shake' — a stand-alone shiver word. The mental back-and-forth sense grew from that image of quivering in place, and nothing else in English descends from it.
Dither means to be indecisive.
The gallery owner dithered over the invitation list for weeks — adding a name each morning, striking two each night — until the printer's deadline passed and the opening went unannounced.
Dither is more damning than 'hesitate': hesitation is a pause before acting, while dithering is fussy, drawn-out indecision that never quite becomes a decision at all.
Dither is the everyday, slightly teasing word for fussing over a choice without landing anywhere.
Its unit-mate vacillate is its formal cousin and swings between definite positions; dithering never even gets that far.

Aunt Renee's bakery opens in three weeks, and it still has no name.

She has narrowed the sign painter's list to two: 'Flour Hour' and 'The Rising.' Each morning she picks one, and by closing time she has talked herself back to the other; the sign painter says she has watched customers dither over birthday cakes with less agony.
Nothing rides on the choice anymore -- suppliers, permits, and menus are all settled -- yet the decision will not land.
Her nephew finally taped both names to the window and told her the town would vote by Friday.
